catalog_quote: ... words to have a closed final syl- lable . In Jahai and one variety of Menriq final syllables are always closed, but several languages including Ceq Wong, Batek, Menriq and Maniq allow words with an open final syllable . Such words are generally less numerous than those with closed syllables, but they are often high - frequency items, as in Ceq Wong sa ' a little ', and galə ' cassava ... Aslian languages, the minimal syllable is [ CV ], and the maximal syllable is usually [ CVC ], or [ CCVC ] for Ceq Wong and Maniq . Syllabification proceeds from right to left, and is maximally exhaustive . In Jahai, for example a string CCCVC will be parsed as /CC.CVC/ . Sequences of consonants are articu- lated with the assistance of an epenthetic vowel, so /CC.CVC/ is [ CVC.CVC ] . The default realisation of the epenthetic vowel is ... final syllable is a glottal segment, / h / or / …
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: It is a principle which can be applied unproblematically to the sample, since the final syllable in most Aslian languages always has the structure /CVC/. The reason for this criterion is that Aslian languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, seldom have suffixes, and the end of the word is therefore usually part of the root and not affected by synchronic or diachronic morphophonemic processes. Also, the final syllable is the most informative part of a word in that it always receives stress and contains the greatest phonemic variation (Diffloth 1976: 102, p.c.).
new_statements.citation: Dunn, Michael, Niclas Burenhult, Nicole Kruspe, Sylvia Tufvesson & Neele Becker. 2011. Aslian linguistic prehistory: a case study in computational phylogenetics. Diachronica 28(3):291-323.
new_statements.locator: p. 300, sec. 2.4 'Cognate coding' (sample incl. Batek Deq, Batek Teq, Batek Teh: Table 1, p. 299)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: (1) Quote check:, PDF page 10 = journal p. 300, sec. 2.4 'Cognate coding' ( lines 403-408). The quoted passage ('It is a principle which can be applied unproblematically to the sample, since the final syllable in most Aslian languages always has the structure /CVC/.... Also, the final syllable is the most informative part of a word in that it always receives stress and contains the greatest phonemic variation (Diffloth 1976: 102, p.c.).') is there verbatim; Table 1 (p. 299) lists Batek Teh Taku, Batek Teh Lebir, Batek Teq, Batek Deq Terengganu, Batek Deq Koh in the sample. I agree this line by itself is a family-level aside attributed to Diffloth, i.e. effectively second-hand for Batek. (2)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement by the Batek fieldworkers themselves (Kruspe, Burenhult): in Aslian languages, including the five Batek varieties in their sample, word stress always falls on the final syllable (the root-final CVC syllable). No Batek-specific first-hand stress statement was found in any opened source; the only open Batek Deq phonology sketch (Rudge 2017) is silent on stress, and the closest sister varieties Jedek (Yager & Burenhult 2017: 508 'Stress falls invariably on the final syllable of words') and Jahai (Burenhult 2005: 38) are described as having invariable, non-contrastive final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Batek; for sister language Jahai, Burenhult 2005: 38 states there is no secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Batek. (Jahai: Malay loans are restressed on the final syllable; Blagden 1906: 773 says Semang generally final but 'in some other dissyllables and polysyllables Semang accents the penultimate'.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, generic across the Aslian family; the statement is made in passing to justify a cognate-coding criterion and is attributed to Diffloth 1976: 102 and p.c., so it is effectively second-hand and not a description of Batek prosody as such.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted Dunn et al. 2011 line is family-level (all Aslian); their sample covers Batek Deq (Sungai Berua, Terengganu; Kuala Koh, Kelantan), Batek Teq, and Batek Teh Taku/Lebir (the latter classed with Menriq, not Batek proper). Rudge 2017's silent phonology sketch is Batek Deq (btq) of Pahang (Taman Negara area); Tengku Intan Suzila's work is Batek Hep' of Kuala Tahan, Pahang. The sister-variety statements are for Jedek (jede1239; Yager & Burenhult 2017) and Jahai (jeha1242; Burenhult 2005), not Batek.

sources.citation: Yager, Joanne & Niclas Burenhult. 2017. Jedek: a newly discovered Aslian variety of Malaysia. Linguistic Typology 21(3):493-545 (author's copy embedded in Yager 2020, Small-scale multilingualism and language contact in egalitarian foragers, PhD thesis, Lund University).
sources.note: For Jedek (closest sister variety within the Menraq-Batek subbranch, not Batek itself), p. 508 sec. 3.1.4: 'Stress falls invariably on the final syllable of words.' No tone or register.

sources.citation: Burenhult, Niclas. 2005. A grammar of Jahai (Pacific Linguistics 566). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Jahai (sister language) sec. 2.5.1 p. 38: non-contrastive stress invariably on the last syllable, no secondary stress; Malay loans restressed finally. Nothing specific on Batek.

sources.citation: Skeat, W. W. & C. O. Blagden. 1906. Pagan Races of the Malay Peninsula, vol. 2 (language part by Blagden). London: Macmillan.
sources.note: p. 773 'Accent': 'As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable'; 'the accent in Semang is usually on the final syllable, yet in some other dissyllables and polysyllables Semang accents the penultimate'. Generic Semang (incl. East Semang/Pangan = Batek area), not Batek-specific.
